newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebel chief Kabila says no let-up in war.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebel chief Kabila says no let-up in war.

text.p: Zaire rebel leader Laurent Kabila spurned calls on Wednesday for a ceasefire in his drive to unseat President Mobutu Sese Seko.
Kabila, head of the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL), told Reuters by telephone from Zaire's second largest city Lubumbashi the "people are against a ceasefire".
Kabila, whose rebels now control more than half of Africa's third largest country, says he is targeting the capital Kinshasa in a bid to drive the ailing Mobutu from power.

He was responding to remarks by U.N. Secretary General Kofi Annan who appealed on Tuesday to U.N. members to press Kabila to seek a negotiated solution through a ceasefire and sustained talks on the country's future.
"How can I declare a ceasefire when the people are against one? The people do not want a ceasefire, they want an end to this corrupt regime," Kabila said.
"So really it is difficult for anyone to force me to agree to a ceasefire. A ceasefire would be against the people's will," he added.
Kabila, who arrived in Lubumbashi on Monday, said he would address a rally there on Thursday and would meet South African President Nelson Mandela "very, very soon" to discuss the Zaire conflict.
He has remained in seclusion in Lubumbashi since he arrived to mark the capture of the mineral-rich Shaba province but he denied encountering dissent, saying he was busy with urgent issues.
"I have encountered no dissent here. The population is solidly behind me and I will be addressing a rally on Thursday," Kabila said.

Lubumbashi's one million people are awaiting a rally, a victory parade or even a clear glimpse of Kabila, who swept into town on Monday in a Mercedes jeep with dark-tinted windows in the middle of a convoy of soldiers.

The only political show in town was a demonstration by several hundred people who welcomed Kabila but also denounced him for imposing an interim governor on Shaba province instead of holding quick elections here as elsewhere.
But Kabila said the man they supported, incumbent governor Kyungu wa Kumwanza, backed the rebel alliance. He denied reports the man was under house arrest.
"Kyungu cannot give me problems. He is behind me and the alliance just like the rest of the population," Kabila said.

The nationalist Katangese party says Kyungu helped Kabila's rebels to take Lubumbashi with few casualties by persuading the Zaire army to change sides. Critics of the Shaba governor say he is an opportunist trying to jump on the Kabila bandwagon, evidently without success so far.
Kabila said he would travel to South Africa "very, very soon" for consultations with Mandela on the Zaire conflict.
Regional analysts said the South Africa talks would centre on arrangements for face-to-face talks between Kabila and Mobutu.
South African Foreign Minister Alfred Nzo on Tuesday predicted dramatic progress within days in ending the civil war in Zaire and said Kabila could visit soon.
